PART 10 — Cases, Toolkit, FAQ and Sources

10.1 Four Composite Cases

These are composites written for illustration, not real people. Names are invented.

Case 1: Meena and her father (career and marriage pressure). Meena (26) wanted to leave a safe engineering job for design and had begun to like a colleague of another community. Her father, Mr. Raghavan, said: "I am only thinking of your future. After all we have done, you will shame us. If you do this, don't expect us at your wedding." Underneath: he had grown up poor and had built security by sacrifice; the I-am-not was "I am not safe, and I am not a good father if she fails." His fear of community shame was the second layer.
What did not work: Meena complied for two years, then hid things and finally exploded.
What changed things: Meena, with a counsellor's help, said: "Papa, I know you say this because you love me and fear for my safety. I've decided. I'd love your blessing, and I'll show you the plan, the savings and the contract. I won't argue every day, and I'll come on Sundays." Her father, with a friend from church, named his fear; he realised his sacrifice was a gift he had turned into a debt. He did not attend the first meeting but came to the second. Trust took years.
Relational reading: the father moved from control to costly presence; the daughter moved from compliance and rebellion to a clear, loving "no."

Case 2: Arun and Deepa (jealousy called love). Arun said: "I'm jealous because I love you." Over time Deepa stopped seeing friends, handed over her phone, and had her salary go into his account. Whenever she objected: "If you loved me, you wouldn't want secrets." Deepa began to doubt her own memory and judgement.
Reading: Arun's I-am-not was "I am not enough; I will be left." But the pattern (isolation, monitoring, money control, shrinking world) is coercive control, which goes beyond a communication problem.
Response: Deepa spoke to a cousin and a counsellor, kept a private record of incidents, rebuilt contact with friends and opened her own bank account. She told Arun clearly what she would no longer accept and that she wanted joint counselling only if he took responsibility. Arun began individual work on his fear; the relationship changed only when his behaviour did, not his promises. Deepa had a safety plan in case he escalated.
Relational reading: love names the fear and refuses the control; safety comes before reconciliation.

Case 3: Lalitha and her son Joel (a "prodigal" and a rescuer). Joel (24) left his job, borrowed money from friends and drifted into gambling. Lalitha paid his debts three times, called his employers to excuse him, and said: "I can't watch my son suffer." Each rescue ended in anger when he asked again.
Underneath: "If I am not needed, I am nothing." Being the rescuer was her identity; the consequences felt like her own death.
Change: With a support group, Lalitha said: "I love you; I'm not paying any more of your debts. I will pay for a counsellor if you choose one, and I'll be at lunch every Sunday." She cried for weeks. Joel was angry, then hit bottom; months later he asked for the counsellor. She did not say "I told you so."
Relational reading: allowing consequences while staying present, as the father in Luke 15, without rescue and without abandonment.

Case 4: Pastor Samuel and the "covering" (spiritual control). A young couple, Daniel and Ruth, were told by their pastor that taking a job in another city was "stepping out from under covering" and would invite spiritual danger. The pastor believed he was shielding them; privately he feared the church's decline and his own sense of failure if members left.
Response: The couple prayed, asked for reasons, sought a second opinion from an older pastor outside the church, and decided to go, thanking the pastor and staying open to contact. Some in the church cooled toward them.
Relational reading: leadership is service, "not lording it over" (1 Pet 5:3); free consent matters even in spiritual authority. The couple's task was to leave without bitterness and to remain open to the pastor.

10.2 The Quick Test: Is This Care or Control?

AskIf the answer is "yes," it leans toward…
Would I be calm if they chose differently and I was powerless to stop it?Care (if "no," examine my fear)
Is my love the same whether they agree or not?Care
Did I give reasons, listen, and leave room to be wrong?Care
Am I using guilt, silence, comparison, threats, or God's name?Control
Does the issue fit their age and capacity?Care (if "no," control)
Is the risk serious and hard to reverse, or a preference or image?Care (serious) / Control (preference)
Would the other say they feel more free, or more afraid, around me?Care (free) / Control (afraid)

10.3 FAQ

Isn't wanting to protect someone good? Yes. Protection is love when it fits the situation (Part 8). The question is whether it respects their capacity and whether the fear is mine or the danger is real.

What about "tough love"? A firm limit that you keep (no more money, I won't lie for you) can be loving, as long as the warmth remains and the aim is their good. When "tough love" becomes punishment, humiliation or cutting off to make a point, it has become control.

Does the Bible tell parents to use the rod? Proverbs (e.g. 13:24; 22:15) speak of discipline, and traditions differ widely on how to read the "rod": as literal punishment, as guidance, or as a figure of speech. Whatever reading, the same Bible says not to provoke children to anger (Eph 6:4) and warns against harshness (Col 3:21). Discipline that frightens, shames or injures is not what these texts intend, and corporal punishment raises serious concerns in research and law; consult child-development guidance where you live.

If I don't push them, they will fail. They may. Failure is sometimes the only teacher that will be heard. Your job is to stay a safe place to return to, not to guarantee outcomes, which you never could.

Is it sin to say no to my parents? Honouring (kabed) is lifelong, but obedience in Scripture is addressed to children in the home. An adult may decide, respectfully, differently. Where an instruction asks you to violate conscience, "we must obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29) applies.

What if the controlling person will not change? You cannot change them. You can change what you do: limits, distance, third-party support, reduced contact, and in danger, protective steps. Forgiving is possible without trusting or reconciling (see the forgiveness and reconciliation study).

Does the relational gospel say God would never intervene? No. Scripture shows God confronting, warning, sending prophets, allowing consequences and sometimes disrupting lives (Paul on the Damascus road). The point is that His intervention is never manipulation, and does not remove a person's participation; it always aims at relationship.

10.4 Summary

In one page: (1) "Love" that controls is better called emotional blackmail, psychological control, conditional regard, coercive control, enmeshment or paternalism, according to the pattern. (2) Underneath it is usually fear, an I-am-not and an unmet need, with the other person drafted in as the cure. (3) The slide from care to control is gradual, and it is reinforced by relief. (4) God's love is persistent and non-coercive: He invites, tells the truth, allows consequences and waits. (5) We are not forced to choose between controlling and abandoning: we stay, speak truth once, offer help, keep our own boundaries, allow consequences, protect those who cannot protect themselves, and keep the door open. (6) For controllers: name the fear, receive what you need from the Father, and tolerate the anxiety of letting go. (7) Where there is coercive control or abuse, safety and accountability come first.
